question: Further to my question E-001077-161, cigarette smuggling levels remain high. According to a report on the subject in Italy, Greece ranks fourth in Europe for the illicit trade in tobacco products, leading to a loss of tax revenue as well as increased public health risks. Smuggling cigarettes naturally results in their selling price being lowered to well below legal levels, making them more attractive and more easily accessible to the public. 1.
Does the Commission have detailed data about cigarette smuggling in Member States, and the lost profits, and if so, what is the situation in Greece?
How does it intend to combat this phenomenon, which leads to a substantial loss in tax revenue for all Member States? How does it plan to protect consumers?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.7.2024) The Commission does not have information regarding the financial losses suffered by individual Member States as a result of the illicit trade in tobacco products. The fight against the illicit tobacco trade is a priority for the Commission.

It is a central part of the investigative activities of the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), which works closely with the competent authorities in the Member States and third countries to tackle this phenomenon.

In 2023, OLAF investigators took part in multiple operations with customs and law enforcement authorities worldwide to counter tobacco smuggling, preventing losses of over EUR 150 million to the EU and national budgets1.

The EU tobacco traceability system established by Directive (EU) 2014/40/EU2 and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/5743, allows for the monitoring of the movements of legal tobacco products within the EU.

Thanks to the information stored in the system, Member States are able to determine at which point a product is no longer reported in the supply chain and subsequently, take the appropriate measures as necessary. The strong addictiveness of tobacco means that illicit trade may create new demand for legal products.
Consumers initially prevented by their age or budget from purchasing the legal tobacco products can be initiated with illicit products.

By contributing to the reduction of artificially cheap supplies of illegal tobacco products on the EU market, the traceability system established by Directive (EU) 2014/40/EU and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2018/574 prevents the initiation of tobacco consumption and thus, protects the consumers’ public health.
